mechaber.en: [Safeguards] to prevent the [Shabbos] lights from being extinguished. Contianing 5 paragraph: If a candle is placed behind a door, it is forbidden to open the door lest the wind will blow it out, {Rama: (in the regular manner) (Rambam, Perek 5; Mordechai Perek 22; Beis Yosef in the name of the Smag) (however) it is permitted to shut the door. (This is the law regarding a window that is next to a candle on a table)(Mordechai and Beit Yosef in the name of Tosfos and Tur). If it is fixed to the wall behind the door, it is forbidden to open and shut the door in the regular manner, lest the door will knock it and extinguish it, rather one should open and shut the door gently. If it is fixed to the door itself, and by opening and shutting the door the oil is moved nearer or farther from the wick, it is forbidden to open and shut the door. Rema: As for a wax candle, it is permitted to open and shut the door, even though it is fixed to the door. (Beis Yosef)}

And Rabbenu Chananel's explanation has, in my view, three explanations: 1 — what Magen Avraham wrote in letter 5, that the door opens inward and the candle is fixed in the wall in such a way that if he opens the door it will knock and reach the candle and thereby extinguish it — opening is permitted, and per Rabbenu Yeshayah, see there, and as written in letter 4, and if not so it will be explained there. And in the Bach it appears according to this explanation. The second explanation of the Taz — that the door opens outward — it is forbidden to open lest it knock the wall from outside and extinguish the candle, and all the more so to close, for it will also sway, etc., and this is the explanation of the Levush, per the explanation of Rabbenu Chananel that the Magen Avraham brought — to open and to close is forbidden. And it is further possible to explain per Rabbenu Chananel that the candle rests on the lintel and in the wall of the doorway next to the opening of the door — now to open is forbidden lest it extinguish through opening when wind comes, and closing will knock there and sway and extinguish — this is possibly the view of the Magen Avraham there, and therefore it is proven specifically as usual, and the same for Rashi and the first explanation of the Magen Avraham, and if not so it will be explained there. And see the Prisha — it appears per Rabbenu Chananel that closing is forbidden and opening is permitted, and it deals with a candle in the wall next to the opening and closing of the door, that when closing it knocks there, see there, and it requires study, and if not so in Magen Avraham it will be explained further, and as written if not so in letter 2.

turei_zahav.he:
אסור לפתוח הדלת ולנעול כו'. זהו פר"ח שמביא ב"י בשם הרא"ש ושם לא הוזכר נעילה אלא כשפותח הדלת נוקש בכותל כו' וא"כ למה נקט כאן ולנעול דמה איסור יש בנעילה גם בב"י זכר אחר כך בפי' ר"ח הנעילה. ונ"ל שהוא מפרש בענין זה שהנר קבוע בהכותל שהוא אחורי הדלת בענין שהכותל שהדלת תלוי בתוכה היא ארוכה באופן שאם יפתח הדלת בחוזק תחזור הדלת עד הכותל מאחוריה ותנקש בה מחמת חוזק הפתיחה ותתנדנד הכותל ששם הנר וכן אם ינעול בחוזק כשתבא הדלת אל הכותל מצד שלפניה תנקש בה ותנדנד כל הכותל אפי' מצד השני שהיא אחורי' וכ"כ לפרש דברי הרמב"ם שמביא ב"י שיש איסור גם בנעילה ואף שבפי' ר"ח לא זכר רק פתיחה מ"מ חד טעמא הוא עם הנעילה:
אסור לפתחו ולנעלו. משמע דבזה לא מהני פתיחה ונעילה בנחת כיון שהוא בדלת עצמה בקלות ינדנד קצת ויקרב או ירחיק השמן:
ובנר של שעוה כו'. נראה פשוט דאם הוא בענין שיש לחוש שיכבה לגמרי אפי' של שעוה אסור:
turei_zahav.en:
It is forbidden to open or close the door, etc. This is Rabbeinu Chananel's explanation, which the Beit Yosef cites in the name of the Rosh. There, however, closing the door is not mentioned. It says only that when one opens the door it strikes the wall, etc. Why, then, does the text here also mention closing it, and what prohibition would there be in closing? The Beit Yosef later also mentions closing in his presentation of Rabbeinu Chananel's explanation. It appears to me that he understands the case as follows. The lamp is fixed in the wall behind the door. The wall in which the door is hung extends far enough that when the door is opened forcefully, it swings back against the wall behind it and strikes it because of the force of the opening, causing the wall on which the lamp stands to shake. Likewise, if the door is closed forcefully, when it reaches the wall in front of it, it strikes that wall and causes the entire wall to shake, even on its rear side. The Rambam's ruling cited by the Beit Yosef can be explained similarly, so that closing is also forbidden. Although Rabbeinu Chananel mentions only opening, closing is forbidden for the same reason.
It is forbidden to open or close it. This implies that here opening or closing gently does not help. Since the lamp is attached to the door itself, even gentle movement will cause it to shake slightly and will bring the oil nearer to or farther from the wick.
And regarding a wax candle, etc. It is obvious that if there is reason to fear that it will be completely extinguished, even a wax candle is forbidden.

biur_halacha.en:
On the board. See Mishnah Berurah, where I wrote that the same applies to a table with candles. Although Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Perishah brings that a table is important and never becomes a basis for a lamp, I did not state this plainly, because from Bach, Taz, Magen Avraham, and many other later authorities it appears they do not hold so. It is surprising that Ba'er Heitev copied from Or Zarua that one may move what is called a shtender even though a wax candle is burning on it, for Or Zarua wrote this only according to Perishah's reasoning. Since Ba'er Heitev first copied the Bach, Taz, and Magen Avraham regarding a table, implying that importance does not prevent it from becoming a basis, the same should apply here.
He shakes off, etc. Although the lamp is thereby moved automatically, it is permitted because this is only tiltul min ha-tzad. But he may not lift the board with the lamp, even after the lamp has gone out, unless he needs the place of the board or it is impossible to shake it off because of loss; then he may lift the board with the lamp to another place, even while it is burning, since after all, where he forgot it, it did not become a basis. All this is explained below in siman 309.
Through a non-Jew. See the Gra, who explains that the reason is concern for the Yerushalmi that is stringent here. It appears from the Rama that even with a wax candle one should be stringent except in pressing circumstances, because it is close to extinguishing; see Hagahot Maimoniyot. But once it has already burned out, all agree that where he forgot it he may shake the board and cause the lamp to fall, even not gently.
It is impossible that he will not bring it nearer, etc. The wording is abbreviated; in truth one should add "or distance it, and he is found to extinguish," as the Rosh brings from the Yerushalmi. Although this is a psik reisha that is not desired, because that extinguishing gives him no benefit since the oil is spilled and lost, as Hagahot Mordekhai writes, unlike seif 1 where the lamp is behind the door and the oil remains for him after extinguishing, and we rule that all agree he is exempt from a chatat, as Magen Avraham writes in siman 320 s.k. 21, nevertheless most poskim hold it is forbidden.
Since he does not move the lamp. The language is difficult, for the board is a basis and moving it should also be forbidden. The main permission is that the board too is not moved, since the case is where it is fixed, as the Taz writes. Even if we explain that the Rama permits even a hanging board, because any swaying is tiltul min ha-tzad since he does not intend actual swaying, as implied in Or Zarua and as I copied above in siman 265 in Biur Halacha, the language remains difficult; he should have said, "since he does not move it by hand." See nearby.
And the candles. According to the Taz, who explains that the case is a fixed menorah, it is permitted even with an oil lamp. But if we explain that it is permitted even with a hanging menorah, then it must refer only to a wax candle; otherwise even mere touching would be forbidden, lest the touch cause it to sway and tilt oil toward the wick, making him liable for kindling, as above in siman 265 in the gloss and as Eliyah Rabbah writes in the name of Nachalat Tzvi. I later examined the Mordekhai in Kol Kitvei, and it implies that the case is fixed, like the Taz, for he writes there that one may touch the stand before the aron kodesh; see there.

machatzit_hashekel.en:
Seif katan 5: The door strikes, etc. It touches the lamp. This excludes the Taz’s interpretation that the lamp is fixed to the wall containing the doorway, though not directly behind the door, and that forcefully opening or closing the door shakes the wall and may extinguish the lamp. Magen Avraham follows Rivash and explains that the lamp is attached directly to the back of the door. On this reading, closing the door is permitted.
Although regarding a bonfire the Shulchan Aruch prohibits opening a door only where an ordinary wind is present, the law of a lamp is stricter according to Rashi. Even an ordinary wind can extinguish a lamp, so opening is prohibited even when no wind is presently blowing, as a safeguard against an ordinary wind. A bonfire, however, is normally extinguished only by an unusual wind. The Sages prohibited an ordinary wind as a safeguard against an unusual one, but did not extend the decree to a place with no wind at all, which would constitute a safeguard upon a safeguard. See citations 514.
